transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-28
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Verdant CTO), Jonas Meyer (Head of ML), Priya Reddy (SRE), Aaron Liu (PM)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Quick scoping for a POC focused on cost modeling and unit economics for Verdant's summarization and search augmentation workloads. Discussed target throughput, average tokens per request, latency SLOs, and budget constraints. Agreed on next steps: send pricing sheet, customer to provide workload sample, schedule benchmark run.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): All right, everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on this account. Quick roll call - you'll see Diego and Ravi from our SE team. Elena, do you want to kick off with a quick overview of the use case?

[00:12] Elena (Verdant): Yeah hi, thanks. So Verdant's use case is basically customer support summarization and a search re-ranker for internal docs. We're planning a phased roll-out, start with internal docs then customer-facing triage. Key constraints are cost - we have a pretty tight budget for inference - and latency: we want sub-300ms p95 for the UI flows.

[00:30] Jonas (Verdant): To add, our expected load initially is around 200 qps peak for internal usage, maybe 50 qps sustained. For customer-facing it's lower but must be highly reliable. Average tokens per call: prompt ~80 tokens, generation ~120 tokens so total ~200 tokens per request on average.

[00:48] Diego (Redwood SE): Cool, that gives us a lot to work with. For the POC do you want us to model hosted API pricing or a Dedicated pool? There's a tradeoff. Hosted is faster to get started, Dedicated is better unit economics at scale.

[01:05] Elena: We're evaluating both. For the pilot we prefer hosted - want to validate quality and behavior - but if the numbers look good we could move to Dedicated in production.

[01:18] Maya: Good - so our approach: we'll run a benchmark with your sample traffic, measure p95 latency and token throughput, and produce a cost model with per-token estimates, batching/caching knobs, and a recommended pilot config. Diego, can you walk through the high-level math we typically show?

[01:34] Diego: Sure. Roughly, we break unit economics into a few parts: model compute per-token (in GPU-seconds), effective tokens per second given batching, and cache hit rates from prefix/KV caching which reduce work. On the hosted side we often present a 1k-token normalized unit so customers can compare. For example, with a mid-sized generation model after quantization we might estimate around $0.50 to $0.80 per 1k tokens for hosted inference depending on batch utilization and instance mix - that's approx $0.0005 to $0.0008 per token.

[02:10] Jonas: That range seems a bit wide. Can you map that to our numbers? If we assume 200 tokens per request and 200 qps peak, what's that look like cost-wise?

[02:22] Diego: Quick back-of-envelope: at 200 qps * 200 tokens = 40k tokens/s peak. Times 3600 seconds -> 144M tokens per hour at sustained peak which is high - I might have mis-said, wait - sorry, math slip: 200 qps * 200 tokens = 40k tokens per second, yes. Over an hour that is 144M tokens. If cost is $0.0006 per token, that's $86.4k per hour - which obviously implies we need better batching/caching or Dedicated pricing. For the pilot you won't run sustained peak for hours; your sustained is lower (50 qps), and caching on repeated prefixes for summarization can cut generation by 40-60% often.

[03:00] Elena: Wow that hourly number is alarming, thanks for flagging. So show us how batching and caching change that.

[03:08] Diego: Right. Batching helps increase GPU utilization which lowers effective cost per token. For example, if you can batch 8-16 concurrent requests we often see 2-3x improvement in throughput per GPU and thus 2-3x lower unit cost. Caching is arguably bigger for you: for summarization, if the same document prefix is requested, KV/prefix caching can serve many reads from cache - that reduces generation tokens significantly. If you get a 50% cache hit rate on downstream generations that's 50% less compute.

[03:42] Priya (Verdant SRE): Quick networking Q - if we go Dedicated on VPC will we have to handle peering and NAT? We want to ensure egress costs aren't double-counted.

[03:51] Ravi (Redwood SE): Yep we'll provide a VPC/on-prem runbook. For Dedicated we support customer VPC peering and private endpoints; egress is typically controlled on your side, we'll call out networking requirements in the runbook. For hosted, egress is included in the API price but there are region nuances.

[04:10] Aaron (PM): Can you give a concrete pilot config to test economics? Like X requests per second, Y model, Z batching.

[04:18] Diego: Proposed pilot: run a 4-hour benchmark using your sample traffic at 3 target loads: low (50 qps), nominal (100 qps), and a short spike test at 200 qps. Use model "redwood-medium-gen-v1" - approximate parity with open medium-sized LLM, run in int8 quantized profile. We'll test three batching configs: batch size 4, 8, 16, and measure p50/p95 latencies and tokens/sec. Also enable prefix/KV caching with a simulated 0%, 25%, 50% hit rate to see delta.

[04:50] Jonas: Sounds good. What's the expected latency impact of batching? We need p95 < 300ms.

[05:00] Diego: Batching increases throughput but can add queueing latency. Our smart routing aims to keep p95 below SLO by dynamically choosing between lower-latency instances and batching pools. From prior runs: with batch size 8 and a tuned queueing window we can keep p95 in the 150-300ms range depending on model and sequence length. For your avg 200 tokens that's doable but borderline at high QPS; that's why we test Dedicated variants that give headroom.

[05:30] Elena: Is quantization going to affect output quality for summarization? We care about hallucinations and concise outputs.

[05:38] Diego: Good point. We include quality checks in the benchmark: run your eval prompt set and measure Rouge/ROUGE-like metrics and a small human spot check. On many models int8/4-bit quantization has minimal impact on summarization quality, but we should validate with your prompts. If quality regresses, we can move to mixed precision or non-quantized on a smaller number of servers for that route.

[06:02] Maya: For cost modeling in the deliverable we'll provide a matrix: cost per 1k tokens for hosted (with typical batching and cache assumptions), cost per 1k tokens for Dedicated committed SKUs (monthly reserved) and an example monthly bill for a few scale points.

[06:18] Jonas: Can you give an example Dedicated number? What does unit cost look like with reserved capacity?

[06:25] Diego: Ballpark: Dedicated with a 12-month commit for a GPU pool running the same quantized model can drop effective unit cost by 40-60% compared to hosted, depending on utilization. So that $0.0006/token could go to $0.00025-0.00036/token. But you need utilization - if you only use it a few hours a week the math breaks. We'll include sensitivity to utilization.

[06:52] Priya: For the POC, we have strict SOC2 and audit log needs. Can you document data retention and KMS integration?

[07:00] Maya: Yes we'll attach our security doc. For Hosted we have options: redact logs, shorten retention; for Dedicated you control keys and audit logs. We'll include a security appendix with the deliverable.

[07:14] Elena: On timelines - how long to get a hosted pilot running vs Dedicated?

[07:21] Maya: Hosted: we can kick off within a couple business days once we get API keys and workload sample. Benchmark run can be scheduled within a week. Dedicated: typical time is 4-6 weeks for reserved capacity and VPC setup depending on procurement and networking. We'll aim to validate hosted first, then decide on Dedicated.

[07:38] Aaron: For the pilot cost we need a capped budget of $15k for evaluation. Can you show a configuration that fits?

[07:45] Diego: Yes - we can do a scoped bench within $15k. For example, a 4-hour benchmark at three load points plus a few follow-up runs and a small synthetic ramp will fall well under $15k on hosted. We'll outline exact SKU usage in the pricing sheet.

[08:02] Jonas: Want to audit the per-token math. Can we go through one concrete scenario? Low-sustained: 50 qps, avg 200 tokens, cache 40% hit, batch size 8, hosted cost baseline $0.0006/token.

[08:18] Diego: Ok. Raw tokens/s = 50*200 = 10k tokens/s. Effective tokens after 40% cache hit -> 6k tokens/s. Hourly tokens = 6k * 3600 = 21.6M tokens/hr. At $0.0006/token that's $12.96k/hr - hmm that again sounds high because $0.0006 * 1M = $600, so 21.6M * $0.0006 = $12,960/hr. But note: hosted pricing is often tiered and our $0.0006 is an upper example; typical per-1k tokens pricing can be per input vs generation and we also account for batching gains; I want to caveat that these numbers are illustrative. For a scoped POC we compute actual observed tokens and multiply by exact hosted SKU prices in the sheet.

[09:02] Elena: Maybe I'm misunderstanding scale - we don't plan sustained 50 qps for hours, these are peaks. Our monthly run-rate is more modest. But for POC it's important to show worst-case.

[09:13] Maya: We'll include three billing scenarios: worst-case sustained peaks, realistic steady-state, and discounted Dedicated projection. We'll show both hourly and monthly extrapolations and sensitivity to cache hit rate and batching.

[09:28] Aaron: Any recommended knobs besides batch size and cache?

[09:31] Diego: A few: 1) Quantization profile (int8 vs fp16) 2) Model family - smaller architecture with similar quality (distillation) 3) Response length caps and safety truncation to hard-limit generation tokens 4) Prefix caching and reuse policies 5) Intelligent routing (send low-latency critical requests to smaller non-batched fleet and bulk to batch pool). We'll include recommended defaults.

[09:58] Jonas: For routing, how does automatic fallback work in congestion?

[10:02] Ravi: Our smart router has policy tiers: if batch pools get overloaded it kicks to a lower-latency reserved pool or to a different model variant. We can plug in cost vs latency rules - e.g., allow 10% of requests to incur higher cost to preserve p95. This reduces failure/retry costs as well.

[10:20] Elena: Regarding QA, we want a small eval harness. Can you run automatic regression checks against our control prompts during bench?

[10:27] Diego: Absolutely. We'll integrate your control set and compute a small suite of metrics (BLEU/Rouge-ish and policy checks). We'll flag any deviations in the deliverable.

[10:36] Maya: Logistics: Jonas - can you upload 1k anonymized queries and 50 eval prompts to the shared folder after the call?

[10:43] Jonas: Yes I can do that by Friday.

[10:46] Elena: A few more questions on procurement: if we choose Dedicated, what's commitment flexibility? 12 vs 6 months?

[10:54] Maya: We do 12 month discounts as standard; we can also propose a 6-month pilot commit but price will be higher. We'll include both in the sheet.

[11:03] Priya: On observability - will we get token-level cost breakdown and traces?

[11:08] Ravi: Yes Redwood Console offers per-route cost, token breakdown, and traces tied to requests. For Dedicated we can increase retention and integrate with your logging stack.

[11:18] Aaron: Can you include a best-practice for reducing token counts in prompts? We're looking for example prompt engineering tradeoffs.

[11:25] Diego: Sure - in the deliverable we include prompt templates that reduce prompt length (structured instructions, slot-filling) and caching-friendly formats (document IDs + offsets rather than full doc text). Small changes can cut prompt tokens by 20-40% in many setups.

[11:40] Jonas: One more number ask: for the pilot, give me expected cost per 1k tokens after batching and 40% cache hit.

[11:47] Diego: If baseline hosted is $0.0006/token -> $0.6 per 1k tokens. With batching + utilization improvements we sometimes show an effective drop to $0.00035/token -> $0.35 per 1k tokens, and with 40% cache hit that effective cost reduces further to about $0.21 per 1k tokens. But again these are illustrative - we will compute exact numbers from bench logs.

[12:12] Elena: That framing helps.

[12:17] Maya: To recap next steps - we will: 1) send POC pricing and recommended bench configs (Maya) 2) SEs to produce test plan and batching/caching configs (Diego/Ravi) 3) Verdant to share sample queries and eval prompts (Jonas) 4) schedule bench week and follow-up review (everyone).

[12:34] Jonas: Sounds good. Anything else on compliance?

[12:37] Maya: We'll attach the SOC2 appendix and KMS integration notes. Also, action item: Priya to confirm network constraints.

[12:45] Priya: Will do.

[12:48] Elena: Thanks everyone - if we stick to the $15k pilot cap please call it out in the pricing.

[12:54] Maya: Will do, we'll give an option that fits the $15k cap and a slightly expanded one.

[13:00] Aaron: Great. Thanks all.

End of meeting.
